title: ERCOT votes to streamline process for data centers looking to join the power grid | Houston Public Media
content:
The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) voted Tuesday to streamline its process for data centers looking to connect to the power grid.
The vote comes as ERCOT is wading through a massive backlog of data centers and other large energy users — such as cryptocurrency miners and industrial facilities — looking to join the grid.
In the past, these so-called "large loads" would go to their local utility company and ask to join the power grid. However, with so many data centers looking to connect, that’s no longer feasible.
It’s hard to evaluate whether there’s enough transmission equipment — such as power lines and transformers — to connect a data center to the grid in a given area, when other nearby projects are constantly being proposed.
"That sequential evaluation of projects was growing untenable," said Bryan Clark, a partner at the global energy law firm Bracewell LLP's Dallas office.
Now, ERCOT is planning to evaluate data centers in batches, rather than individually. Its board voted to move forward with the first combined study of data centers, known as "Batch Zero," on Tuesday. The new process will now go to the Public Utility Commission of Texas for approval on June 18.
"Batch Zero is necessary as ERCOT intends to transition the large load interconnection process from an individual study-based approach to a batch study-based approach that allocates available transmission capacity for studied and committed large loads," ERCOT said in a statement to Houston Public Media.
The new process has drawn widespread interest from technology leaders looking to develop in Texas, who have provided hours of public comment to ERCOT.
"There's been a lot of time and effort by both ERCOT staff and stakeholders to solve an issue that is frankly critical for the Texas economy," Clark said.
In the first few months of this year, nearly 200 data centers and other large energy consumers requested to join the grid. They're seeking a combined 438 gigawatts of power in Texas — more than five times the amount of energy used to power the entire state during record-breaking demand. However, energy experts said that number is likely inflated by facilities that may never be built.
The new process for evaluating data centers aims to weed out more speculative projects that may never be built in Texas. While ERCOT is still workshopping its criteria for joining Batch Zero, those criteria could include factors such as whether a proposed data center project already has the land and financing to build.
"You're going to have a more predictable system in which projects that can and will be built will be connected to the grid on a more rational basis," Clark said.

title: Duke Energy upgrades underground power grid in downtown St. Pete to boost reliability
content:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. - Deep beneath the bustling streets of downtown St. Petersburg, a massive network of specialized electrical equipment ensures continuous power for the city.
Duke Energy upgrades downtown St. Petersburg
What we know:
Duke Energy crews swarmed the area Wednesday to replace aging cables with new ones as a proactive measure.
Thick insulated power cables are fed directly into an underground utility access point beneath the city streets.
"The system kind of self-heals itself," Torean Savage, a network specialist with Duke Energy, said. "So, if one place goes out of power, there's another transformer and cables making up for that power, preventing outages or kind of fixing the outage at a faster rate of speed."
While some above-ground lines have this self-healing technology too, the big deal with this network is it’s protected from the elements and won’t get corroded by water.
Grid reliability history
The backstory:
The network has been in downtown St. Pete since the 1950s, replacing the traditional above-ground power lines that have to be a certain distance from public spaces for safety purposes. That’s clearance that downtown St. Pete and many other cities don’t have.
Traditional overhead power lines stretch across a utility pole, illustrating the older style of electrical distribution that requires public clearance.
About half of Duke Energy’s power lines across Florida are underground, and the other half are overhead. Normal underground power lines, though, are different than this network. They can’t get wet and still work, while this submersible system can.
Weatherproofing local communities
What they're saying:
"It’s definitely a game-changer. Like I said, if you've been around for these hurricanes and storms going around, it definitely helps with the reliability," Savage said.
A Duke Energy utility vehicle stands ready on a city street with a massive spool of heavy-duty electrical cable during infrastructure upgrades.
The technology is only in two places, downtown St. Pete and downtown Clearwater, out of the company’s 35-county territory.
"We have hospitals here. We have the airport right here, government buildings. We want to make sure those places are protected," Savage said.
Expanding the grid
What's next:
Savage says that the company hopes to expand this type of network to other areas.
The Source: The information in this story was gathered from Duke Energy network specialist Torean Savage, who explained how the underground power grid operates.

title: In Massachusetts, parked EVs will start feeding the grid this summer
content:
Next Upcoming
Canary Live Bay Area
By Canary Media
After the school year ends in the Massachusetts towns of Acton and Boxborough, the district’s electric buses will mostly stay put in a parking lot. But they won’t sit idle all summer.
The three vehicles will charge up their nearly 200-kilowatt-hour batteries overnight, when the power supply is at its cleanest and cheapest, then send energy back to the grid from 4 p.m. to 7 p.m. on days when the grid is strained. The district will earn revenue for the power it shares, perhaps even enough to cover the costs of charging up during the school year, said Kate Crosby, energy manager for the Acton-Boxborough school district. Plus, the strategy will help lower the emissions and cost of the region’s electricity supply.
“The more we plug in batteries to the grid, the less we use peaker plants,” Crosby said. “They will help to stabilize the grid, help to reduce the cost of electricity for all ratepayers, and they’ll help make the grid cleaner.”
Acton-Boxborough’s school buses are the first vehicles to plug in to a Massachusetts program that aims to demonstrate and investigate the potential of “vehicle-to-everything” technologies, more commonly known as V2X. These systems use bidirectional chargers, which can power up a vehicle as well as send the energy stored in an EV’s battery back to a building or the grid.
Supporters say V2X technologies can yield a host of benefits. They can lower emissions by using stored energy generated at times when the grid is consuming less fossil fuel. They can help users offset their electricity bills by compensating them for power sent to the grid. They contribute to resilience when the power goes out. Plus, they can keep prices lower for everyone by sending cheaper power to the grid during times of high demand.
So far, however, widescale adoption has been elusive. Pilot programs across the U.S. and abroad have tested the possibilities, but they haven’t gained much traction in the face of high upfront costs, technical complexity, the huge variation among what equipment works with what vehicles, and the lack of established plans to compensate users for the power they pour back into the grid.
Massachusetts hopes its initiative will make some headway against these obstacles. At an event last week, the planners behind the demonstration program discussed what they’ve achieved so far, what they’ve learned along the way, and what problems remain.
The Massachusetts Clean Energy Center, an economic development agency, announced the demonstration program in early 2025, with the goal of giving away up to 100 bidirectional chargers to a variety of users. Participants were announced in February 2026: five school districts, four municipalities, and 30 residents. In order to understand how the systems function in a wide range of settings, the planners selected projects in all geographical corners of the state, and in rural, urban, and suburban areas served by 10 different utilities. The installations will include six different types of chargers plugging into eight different vehicles, from buses and pickup trucks to SUVs and compact hatchbacks.
“It’s not just about getting the right vehicle and the right chargers,” said Sally Griffith, transportation electrification program manager for energy consulting firm Resource Innovations, which is working with the state to run the program. “It’s about the whole system — how all of this needs to work together,” she said at the event.
Between 10 and 15 chargers are now installed and awaiting authorization to begin bidirectional charging. The rest are expected to be online by September.
Already, some challenges have been identified. The most pressing, speakers at the event said, have to do with finding a financial model that works.
For one, the systems are pricey: $15,000 to $40,000 for a residential setup, the Massachusetts Clean Energy Center estimates. Pilot programs can help defray costs for small numbers of users for a limited time, but a long-term, reliable compensation plan is needed to get any meaningful number of EV owners to make the leap.
But it turns out those compensation programs can be tricky to design. In Massachusetts, one major discovery so far has been the conflict between state solar incentives and the ConnectedSolutions program, which compensates battery owners for sending power onto the grid. Existing technology can’t tell the difference between electrons sent from solar panels and those coming from batteries. For a home with both solar panels and a bidirectional charger, it would be impossible to separate the solar power that should receive net-metering incentives from the EV battery power that would receive payment from ConnectedSolutions.
The Massachusetts Clean Energy Center had to immediately disqualify roughly 75% of the nearly 300 residential applicants for the V2X program because their homes had solar power, said Elijah Sinclair, the center’s senior program manager.
The state was aware there might be a conflict, but the scale took program planners by surprise, delaying the selection of participants and therefore the deployment of chargers.
One possible answer could lie in a program that compensates virtual power plants — networks of distributed energy resources like solar panels, batteries, and demand management — rather than providing different incentives for each component of the system, Steve Letendre, senior adviser at the Vehicle-Grid Integration Council, an EV charging advocacy group, told event attendees.
“We believe it’s a mechanism by which we can bring EVs onto the grid in a way that maximizes their value,” he said.
An unexpected bright spot so far has been the ease of interconnection, the process of formalizing agreements with utilities for hooking up an energy resource to the grid, Sinclair said.
“Utility interconnection was expected to be a big barrier,” he said. “But everyone has been just awesome to work with, and interconnection hasn’t slowed us down.”
The Massachusetts Clean Energy Center will collect data from participants for the rest of the year. By the end of the year, it aims to publish a comprehensive guidebook on what it’s learned about the cost, system design, and technical and regulatory barriers, with the goal of helping other agencies and states replicate the program.
In the meantime, the students and bus drivers of Acton-Boxborough will be enjoying quieter rides without any diesel fumes, said Crosby, the district energy manager.
“We are improving their quality of life immediately, and helping to create a cleaner, more stable future for them,” she said. “There’s nothing that matters more to us.”

title: Securing a Reliable Power Grid - Powerlines
content:
There’s a lot that goes on behind the plugs that power your life.
We work every day to improve the reliability of our electrical system. It starts at our generating facilities and continues across hundreds of miles of our overhead transmission and distribution power lines. At each step along the way, we’re working to improve reliability for the communities we serve.
Generator Upgrades Extend Their Life Up to 40 Years
Did you know that over 80% of our energy supply comes from the natural power of Pacific Northwest rivers? Hydropower generators make this happen. Like any appliance or even your car, generators need regular maintenance to keep working efficiently.
We’re currently working on a major overhaul of three generators at Boundary Dam. All three generators are original to Boundary Dam and have been in use for nearly 60 years. For the overhaul, crews are rebuilding aging infrastructure and redesigning components for each generator. We’re also replacing the transformers that prepare the power generated by each generator for transmission.
We started the overhaul project in 2019 and expect to wrap things up next year. Once complete, the overhaul will help extend the life of the generators for nearly 40 additional years. We’ll also be able to generate up to 60 more megawatts of power than before. This is crucial to help improve reliability and meet the increasing electrical needs of our customers.
Vegetation Management Along Transmission Lines Keeps Power Flowing
After the power leaves our generating facilities, it travels across the state of Washington along high-voltage transmission lines. The vegetation under those transmission lines, from grassy meadows to trees, has to be maintained to safely deliver energy to our service area.
Our right of way and powerline clearance crews monitor trees and brush near these high voltage lines and remove vegetation as needed. They perform required clearing each year in compliance with federal electric and environmental rules. This work helps reduce the chance of power interruptions, wildfires, and safety hazards.
They even use technology and 3D modeling to spot risks from vegetation. This is especially helpful when monitoring lines that are hard to get to on foot. Near our Boundary Dam, for example, crews recently used 3D modeling to locate overgrown vegetation. Once identified, we hired crews to repel down the rock face outside the dam and clear the vegetation from the lines.
Distribution Technology Helps Isolate Power Outages
The reliability metric most folks are familiar with is unplanned power outages. It makes sense: A reliable system will have fewer and shorter outages compared to an unreliable one. While we can’t predict when unplanned outages will happen, we can prepare for them.
One way we’re preparing is by installing smart switches on the power lines across our service area. These devices help isolate the failed equipment and restore power to the unaffected areas within minutes. You can think of this like a string of decorative lights. When one bulb goes out, only that bulb is out while the rest of the string continues to shine.
In 2015, we started adding smart switches to our distribution lines in places with higher risks to outages. This includes areas with heavy tree cover like Lake Forest Park and areas where power is essential for life-saving organizations like Seattle Children’s. To date, we’ve installed about 80 switches across our distribution system. These efforts combined help improve our service reliability and deliver the power you need every day.

title: The rise of distributed energy and power grid | Political Economy | thenews.pk
content:
The path ahead lies in aligning the power system with the realities of an increasingly decentralised energy future
| A | 
mid the ongoing global energy transition, mainly driven by the rise of distributed energy resources, Pakistan is charting a decentralised path, where a bottom-up solar revolution is reshaping the power system. There has been a notable rise in distributed energy with solar (estimated at 18-20 GW by the government and up to 33 GW by Policy Research Institute for Equitable Development) and a battery boom already under way.
There is no doubt that this transition has improved access and affordability. It is now supplying an estimated 20 to 25 percent of electricity demand and has reduced dependence on imported fuels by nearly 40 percent. Nonetheless, its rapid expansion has generated new concerns for the existing power grid.
The challenge is no longer choosing between grid electricity and distributed energy but making both work within a system that remains reliable, affordable and financially sustainable. This requires redefining the grid from a one-way supply network into a more flexible system that can integrate distributed generation, storage and changing demand. Pakistan’s real reform challenge is how Pakistan manages this transition to strengthen, rather than strain, the power sector.
Yet much of the debate still treats distributed solar as a billing issue, centred on unit rates, export compensation, fixed charges and retail bills, when in fact it is signalling a much deeper shift in how the power sector must function.
The real challenge is not the growth of distributed energy, but whether grid planning, regulation and tariff structures can evolve in time to integrate it efficiently while preserving reliability, utility sustainability and equity across consumers.
The recent regulatory shift from net metering to net billing reflects a growing recognition of emerging technical, financial and equity concerns for the existing system. Under net metering, ‘prosumers’ could export surplus electricity at retail tariffs while drawing from the grid during peak hours, essentially treating it as a virtual storage. This framework played a key role in accelerating early solar adoption. However, it also introduced key concerns regarding cost recovery, cross-subsidisation and operational strain on distribution networks, including power quality concerns and the increasingly visible ‘duck curve.’
The shift to net billing seeks to better align export compensation with the actual system value of surplus generation in a grid where daytime solar abundance does not coincide with peak demand. Framing the issue purely as net metering versus net billing risks oversimplifying a deep structural challenge.
As distributed solar and self-generation continue to expand, the key concern lies between a rigid, cost-heavy utility model and a rapidly evolving demand profile. Net billing may partially address immediate imbalances, but it does not resolve the underlying misalignment in tariff design, cost allocation and system planning.
Lower export tariffs combined with rising fixed charges may unintentionally promote a transition to self-consumption among affluent households and commercial users. As battery costs continue to decline, solar-plus-storage systems are becoming increasingly viable, enabling partial - in some cases near-complete - grid defection. This could enhance resilience among consumers but poses a risk of further eroding the utility revenue base, shifting system costs onto remaining grid-dependent consumers and deepening existing inequities if not addressed through comprehensive reform.
Early indications are already visible. Pakistan imported around 1.25 GWh of lithium-ion battery storage packs in 2024, equivalent to nearly 4.7 percent of that year’s 25.6 GW peak demand, according to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. If deployed at scale under regular charging and discharging cycles, this storage capacity alone could meaningfully reduce annual electricity demand from the grid.
This trajectory increases prices for consumers still dependent on the grid, reduces the base for fixed-cost recovery and exacerbates financial fragility. Even modest shifts to self-generation steadily reduce utilisation of infrastructure designed for predictable demand.
Pricing adjustments alone cannot resolve the structural mismatch between legacy tariff models and an increasingly decentralised electricity market. A tariff structure accurately reflecting grid reliance and ensuring cost recovery is required.
The power sector’s viability rests on aligning tariff policy with evolving consumption patterns and the rising role of distributed generation. Tariff policy must evolve alongside consumption. The increase in protected and lifeline consumers, from 9.4 million to 21.5 million in four years, exposes slab-based limits. Behind-the-meter solar reduces recorded consumption without reflecting income vulnerability. When such households occupy subsidised brackets, fixed costs are shifted to fully grid-dependent users, undermining both equity and revenue.
A more durable approach lies in cost-reflective tariff structures that clearly separate fixed system obligations from variable energy consumption. Capacity and network costs should be recovered through a defined fixed charge linked to grid reliance. Energy tariffs should vary by time of use, lower during solar-rich hours and higher during peak periods to reflect system constraints and readiness costs. Such time-of-use pricing can better align demand with solar generation, reduce evening peak stress, improve system efficiency, strengthen distribution company revenues and minimise embedded cross-subsidies through clearer price signals.
Social protection requires a shift toward vulnerability-based targeting grounded in energy-poverty indicators, focusing on genuinely energy-poor households, including those without grid access. Subsidy design should reflect geographic constraints, structural access limitations and actual need rather than electricity consumption alone. Policy choices between cash transfers and asset-based support should be guided by evidence-based analysis, stakeholder consultation and long-term fiscal sustainability. Such an approach can better protect vulnerable consumers while strengthening energy equity and energy justice and easing both fiscal and system-level pressures on the power sector.
Solar electricity is generated when the sun shines or the wind blows, not necessarily when it is needed. Midday surpluses, curtailment risks and steep evening ramps are structural features of this transition.
As its share rises, distributed solar hollows out average daytime demand (with an annual reduction of around 10 TWh already reported in official estimates). Evening peaks continue to persist after sunset, driven by residential and commercial consumption. The grid remains reliant on conventional generation to meet these peaks, highlighting the need for complementary measures such as energy storage, flexibility markets and demand-side management.
At the network level, grid constraints may prevent distributed resources from achieving their full value. These resources cannot be fully leveraged if the distribution network lacks adequate capacity and real-time coordination.
Surplus daytime solar often remains underutilised or cannot be shifted toward evening peaks, constraining both reliability and economic value. Traditional grid planning approaches struggle to capture the true hosting capacity of modern networks; greater use of real-time data, monitoring and advanced control can unlock additional solar capacity while maintaining system stability.
In this context, grid flexibility is critical. The system must be able to balance variable renewable output (solar and wind), shift demand in real time and deploy storage to maintain reliability without over-reliance on conventional generation. Without such flexibility, variability in renewable supply can quickly translate into system volatility. The challenge is therefore not only to add more generation, but to make the system capable of accommodating a more dynamic and decentralised electricity landscape.
Market design must evolve accordingly. Batteries are already advancing alongside the solar surge; by storing surplus daytime generation and supplying it during evening peaks, they ease the duck curve and reduce strain on conventional power plants. Behind-the-meter battery systems stabilise local networks and optimise self-consumption. Grid-scale batteries can provide frequency support, manage congestion and supply firm peak capacity. To realise these benefits, market design must explicitly value flexibility: ancillary services should be transparently priced and open to storage. Capacity payments should reward responsiveness rather than installed output alone.
Utilities should transition from selling power to managing the system, with compensation tied to reliability, efficient integration of distributed resources and operational performance. This transition, already emerging in several advanced power systems, can be supported through smart grids, digital monitoring and dynamic pricing that enable consumers to participate more actively while preserving system stability.
Peer-to-peer electricity trading can support this transition if grounded in robust regulatory and settlement frameworks. Licensed digital platforms can allow ‘prosumers’ to sell surplus locally, encouraging balancing and reducing unnecessary reverse flows. All transactions must clear through the distribution network with transparent wheeling charges. Smart meters, verified credentials and regulator-supervised settlement mechanisms are essential to ensure accurate measurement and consumer protection.
Such models can unlock value from distributed assets, support community micro-grids and ease pressure on transmission infrastructure, provided it operates within grid codes and financial discipline rather than an informal market detached from system obligations.
Virtual power plants (VPPs) can provide an additional means of large-scale resource aggregation. VPPs provide despatch-able capacity and grid support by combining distributed solar, battery storage and flexible demand, helping the power system to manage variable solar output while reducing stress on conventional infrastructure. However, two important aspects influence their practical impact.
First, VPPs function primarily as rapid-response resources, delivering value during periods of system stress or contingency conditions rather than through continuous market participation. This reflects the economic choices of distributed resource owners, who often prioritise self-consumption and resilience, making event-driven dispatch more attractive.
Second, the potential of VPPs is constrained by the capability and digital readiness of the distribution network. Legacy infrastructure, limited smart meter penetration, and outdated planning frameworks often limit the reliable aggregation and real-time coordination of distributed resources at scale.
Targeted pilot projects can help assess the viability of VPPs, particularly in high density distributed solar zones. Linking these pilots to the evolving Competitive Trading Bilateral Contracts Market can provide practical evidence on how aggregated distributed resources may participate in future market transactions under clear operational limits and grid compliance requirements. Such pilots can guide policymakers and utilities in designing frameworks that integrate distributed generation more effectively while preserving system reliability and market discipline.
The path ahead lies in aligning the power system with the realities of an increasingly decentralised energy future. The core objective is to build a hybrid system in which centralised generation and distributed energy operate in coordinated balance rather than competition. This requires an integrated reform agenda grounded in grid modernisation, tariff restructuring, enabling new market actors and development of flexibility markets, deployment of storage, digital system oversight, modernising distribution models and performance-based regulation.
The objective is not to slow the growth of distributed energy, but to ensure its effective integration into a financially viable and operationally resilient power system. Pakistan’s energy future is not a binary choice between centralised and distributed models; it is inherently hybrid, and its success will depend on how effectively this transition is governed and managed.
Shafqat Hussain Memon is an academic and energy researcher based in Jamshoro.He can be reached at hussainshafqat.memon @gmail.com
Toqueer Ahmed Jumani is an assistant professor in electrical engineering at A’Sharqiyah University, Ibra, Oman.

title: Knowledge-guided multimodal reasoning framework for intelligent power grid maintenance - Scientific Reports
content:
Abstract
Power grid infrastructure maintenance requires reliable integration of heterogeneous data sources including historical fault records, technical documents, and visual inspection imagery. Existing approaches face challenges in ensuring output completeness, consistency verification, and systematic multimodal data integration—critical requirements for high-stakes operational decisions. This paper presents an integrated multimodal reasoning system designed to address these reliability requirements through systematic quality assurance mechanisms. The system architecture comprises three components: (1) a document processing pipeline constructing a structured knowledge base from 10,247 heterogeneous maintenance records (8,198 for training, remaining for validation and testing); (2) a retrieval-augmented reasoning module implementing a Recursive Augmented Thinking (RAT) mechanism with three-dimensional self-evaluation (slot completeness, confidence assessment, logical consistency verification) tailored to power grid fault diagnosis requirements; (3) an attention-enhanced visual detection module for identifying equipment anomalies. Validation on 120 real-world fault cases demonstrates that the RAT mechanism achieves 95% output completeness and 0.82 confidence score through iterative refinement (approximately 98% convergence within 3 iterations), compared to 65% completeness and 0.55 confidence for single-pass generation. Visual detection on 15,648 inspection images achieves 0.952 mAP@.5 with maintained robustness under challenging conditions (87.4% performance retention under occlusion, distance, and adverse weather). These results indicate practical deployment potential within the validated scope of operational power grid maintenance.
Similar content being viewed by others
Introduction
Power grid infrastructure maintenance presents significant operational challenges due to the critical nature of electrical equipment and the severe consequences of failures. Unplanned outages cost approximately $150 billion annually in the U.S.1, while equipment degradation poses ongoing safety risks2. Maintenance decision-making currently faces three operational challenges: (1) dependence on expert diagnosis that is time-intensive and subject to inter-operator variability3; (2) fragmented data sources—historical fault records, technical specifications, visual inspection imagery—processed through isolated workflows that lack systematic integration; (3) static knowledge systems requiring manual reconfiguration as operational standards evolve, creating potential gaps between documented procedures and current requirements.
Recent advances in natural language processing and computer vision provide technical capabilities for processing heterogeneous industrial data4,5. Large language models (LLMs), combined with retrieval-augmented generation architectures, offer potential solutions for integrating textual and visual information streams6,7,8.
Motivation for retrieval-augmented language models
Retrieval-augmented LLMs offer four practical capabilities for grid maintenance: (1) natural-language processing of heterogeneous formats (reports, manuals, images) without custom integration pipelines; (2) external-retrieval-based domain adaptation, avoiding full retraining when standards evolve; (3) structured outputs with intermediate reasoning that supports operator verification; (4) instruction-tuning to new equipment/fault patterns with limited labels.
From a broader cyber-physical reliability perspective, maintenance intelligence must be evaluated by data trustworthiness, communication availability, and attack resilience in addition to prediction quality. Recent CPS reliability studies emphasize FDI mitigation and reliability-aware operation under sensing/communication uncertainty9,10; PMU and synchrophasor research highlights placement, cybersecurity, and communication-degradation impacts on DTR/SIPS workflows11,12,13,14; survey-level evidence confirms that ICT integration reshapes power-system reliability boundaries15,16. Complementary engineering studies on grid-tied renewable optimization and learning-based forecasting/control further inform our domain-aware design17,18,19.
However, applying general-purpose LLMs to high-stakes industrial maintenance contexts requires addressing several operational requirements20,21. Generic models lack domain-specific knowledge about electrical equipment specifications, diagnostic protocols, and safety regulations. Power grid maintenance further requires specific capabilities beyond general language understanding: (1) Output completeness verification—ensuring all mandatory decision-support fields (fault cause, affected components, maintenance actions, risk assessment, reference basis) are populated before operator review; (2) Logical consistency checking—validating that generated recommendations align with domain constraints (e.g., correlating gas analysis patterns with appropriate fault mechanisms); (3) Multimodal information integration—incorporating both textual knowledge and visual inspection evidence for comprehensive diagnostics; (4) Traceability and auditability—providing explicit citations to source documents for expert verification.
Existing retrieval-augmented generation approaches provide external knowledge integration but typically employ single-pass generation without systematic quality assessment22,23. While methods such as Self-Refine24 and CRITIC25 introduce iterative improvement, they lack structured evaluation dimensions tailored to domain-specific requirements (e.g., mandatory field completeness, domain rule consistency). Similarly, visual anomaly detection methods26,27 face challenges with small or distant objects in complex backgrounds, and typically operate in isolation without systematic integration with textual diagnostic knowledge.
Weaknesses in Existing Literature
Prior studies reveal three persistent gaps for operational deployment: (i) fragmented treatment of cyber reliability and maintenance reasoning, where communication/data integrity risks are analyzed separately from diagnostic generation quality; (ii) limited output governance, with incomplete or weakly verifiable structured recommendations in high-stakes settings; (iii) weak coupling between text-centric and vision-centric modules, reducing end-to-end robustness in heterogeneous field conditions.
Motivation
These gaps motivate an integrated system architecture that: (1) constructs a structured domain knowledge base from heterogeneous maintenance records; (2) implements systematic quality assurance through multi-dimensional evaluation tailored to power grid operational requirements; (3) integrates textual reasoning and visual detection capabilities for comprehensive fault diagnosis.
This study addresses the research question: “ How can heterogeneous maintenance data be systematically integrated into a quality-assured reasoning framework that meets operational reliability requirements for power grid fault diagnosis?” Figure 1 summarizes the end-to-end architecture: (i) offline knowledge-base construction transforming heterogeneous maintenance documents into a dual-indexed structured repository; (ii) online retrieval-augmented reasoning producing five-slot maintenance strategies under the RAT quality-assurance loop; (iii) attention-enhanced visual inspection detecting equipment anomalies. The three stages share the same domain knowledge base. Experimental validation on 120 real-world fault cases and 15,648 inspection images from operational substations demonstrates the system’s practical viability.
Novelty statement
Unlike prior retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems that adopt single-pass or generic self-refinement loops without domain-tailored quality constraints, and unlike prior power-grid AI works that treat textual reasoning and visual inspection as isolated pipelines, this paper introduces three jointly designed innovations that are, to the best of our knowledge, novel: (i) a domain-specific three-dimensional self-evaluation mechanism (mandatory five-slot completeness, weighted confidence, and rule-based logical consistency) that is explicitly aligned with power-grid operational protocols rather than reused from general-purpose RAG critiques such as Self-Refine and CRITIC; (ii) a quality-triggered hierarchical refinement policy (knowledge gap \(\succ\) low confidence \(\succ\) logical inconsistency) that selectively regenerates only deficient slots, achieving 98% convergence within 3 iterations versus uncontrolled iteration budgets used by Self-Refine; (iii) an end-to-end multimodal integration that couples the same structured knowledge base with both the RAT reasoning module and an ACmix-enhanced YOLOv7 inspection module, supporting joint textual–visual diagnosis under cyber-physical operating conditions including communication degradation and partial sensor availability. Our specific contributions and novelty are:
- 
                    1.
                    
                      Novel quality-assured multimodal data integration pipeline: A document processing workflow combines layout analysis (PP-PicoDet), text recognition (RARE), named entity recognition (PMRC), and defect classification (MASKER) to construct a structured knowledge base from 10,247 heterogeneous maintenance documents (yielding 1,083 structured knowledge entries). The pipeline is, to our knowledge, the first to combine these four modules with explicit cyber-physical data-trustworthiness checks (cross-source consistency verification and provenance tagging) for power-grid maintenance corpora. This pipeline addresses challenges of variable document quality (68% scanned PDFs, 72-600 DPI), irregular layouts (55% multi-column), and domain-specific terminology under degraded conditions, achieving 94.3% layout accuracy and 91.7% character-level recognition accuracy—improvements of \(+15.0\) and \(+13.4\) percentage points respectively over generic OCR baselines reported in our experiments.
- 
                    2.
                    
                      Novel quality-assured retrieval-augmented reasoning with recursive domain-tailored evaluation: To address operational requirements for output completeness and consistency verification in power grid maintenance decision support, we implement a Recursive Augmented Thinking (RAT) mechanism combining retrieval-augmented generation with systematic self-evaluation and iterative refinement. In contrast to Self-Refine24 and CRITIC25, which apply free-form critiques without structured operational targets, RAT employs three evaluation dimensions tailored to power grid fault diagnosis operational requirements: (i) mandatory field completeness verification ensuring all five required slots (fault cause, affected component, maintenance actions, risk level, reference basis) are populated; (ii) content quality assessment via weighted confidence scoring (\(\text {Confidence} = 0.4 \cdot C_{slot} + 0.3 \cdot C_{detail} + 0.3 \cdot C_{certain}\)); (iii) logical consistency checking validating alignment between fault indicators and recommended actions using domain rule patterns. Empirical evaluation on 120 real-world cases demonstrates 95% output completeness and 0.82 confidence score through iterative refinement (approximately 98% convergence within 3 iterations), compared to 65% completeness and 0.55 confidence for single-pass generation baseline—a relative improvement of \(+46\%\) in completeness and \(+49\%\) in confidence.
- 
                    3.
                    
                      Novel attention-enhanced visual detection coupled with textual reasoning: An ACmix-augmented YOLOv7 architecture addresses operational challenges of small-scale defect detection (objects <32\(^2\) pixels constituting 38% of dataset) and distant inspection scenarios (50–200 m range). Beyond a single-modality detector, our design is the first in the power-grid maintenance literature (to our knowledge) to share a unified structured knowledge base with the upstream RAT reasoning module, enabling joint textual–visual diagnosis. The hybrid attention mechanism combining convolutional local feature extraction and self-attention global context modeling achieves 0.950 precision and 0.952 mAP@.5 on 15,648 inspection images, with maintained robustness under challenging conditions (\(87.4\%\) average performance retention under 30-70% occlusion, extreme lighting, and adverse weather)—a \(+4.6\)-point mAP gain over the YOLOv7 baseline and a \(+11.6\)-point gain on small-object mAP.
Related work
Retrieval-augmented generation and quality assurance
Recent advances include RAG22 for knowledge incorporation, CoT23 for reasoning, Self-Refine24 for iterative improvement, and CRITIC25 for external validation. However, these methods lack systematic multi-dimensional quality assessment tailored for domain-specific structured outputs with operational requirements. For power grid maintenance requiring mandatory information fields and domain rule compliance, this study implements three-dimensional evaluation (field completeness, content quality, logical consistency) within a retrieval-augmented architecture, specifically designed for power grid fault diagnosis with task-specific fine-tuning and iterative quality-assured refinement.
Industrial multimodal diagnostics
Data-driven approaches28,29,30 have shown success with numerical sensor data and single-modality inputs but lack integration of unstructured textual knowledge and interpretability for high-stakes decisions. Object detection methods31,32,33 face challenges with small objects in complex power grid scenarios. This work addresses these gaps through ACMix attention mechanisms for small object detection and multimodal fusion of textual knowledge with visual inspection data.
Grid-tied renewable optimization and learning-based forecasting/control
Beyond pure language-model literature, our framework is methodologically informed by recent advances in optimization, control, and learning-based forecasting on the power-engineering side. The PV/inverter ratio optimization review17 demonstrates that structured multi-objective evaluation (efficiency, cost, reliability) leads to more deployable grid-tied systems—a principle that motivates our three-dimensional output evaluation (completeness, confidence, consistency) rather than monolithic loss minimization. The robust variable-step perturb-and-observe sliding-mode controller for grid-connected wind systems18 shows how adaptive step-size mechanisms maintain stability under varying operating conditions; this directly inspires the adaptive iterative refinement in our RAT loop, where refinement intensity adapts to the detected deficiency type (knowledge gap, low confidence, or logical inconsistency) rather than applying a uniform regeneration step. The radial basis function neural network short-term load forecasting study for super high voltage grids19 highlights the importance of domain-tailored feature representations for high-voltage grid intelligence; analogously, our knowledge base is constructed using domain-tailored layout, OCR, and NER modules rather than off-the-shelf pipelines. Collectively, these works confirm that domain-aware structuring—rather than generic deep models—is essential for trustworthy power-grid AI, motivating the structured, quality-assured design of our framework.
Positioning within cyber-physical reliability literature
Recent CPS reliability research provides the broader context for our system. Data integrity / FDI:9 mitigates false data injection on DLR systems, and10 models DLR reliability across sensing, communication, and control layers. We operationalize the same data-integrity philosophy by attaching cross-source provenance tags and consistency scores to every knowledge entry, so that RAT inherits explicit data-trust labels. PMU/synchrophasor reliability:11 shows that flexibly-rated PMU placement improves observability and reliability;12 surveys PMU-CPS cybersecurity exposure;13,14 quantify how synchrophasor-based DTR/SIPS reliability degrades under composite cyber stress and communication unavailability. The shared insight—reasoning outputs are only as reliable as the underlying observability and communication channels—motivates two RAT design choices: (i) the consistency dimension flags outputs depending on degraded sensor families, and (ii) iterative refinement re-retrieves alternative evidence when primary channels are unreliable. Survey-level CPS reliability:15,16 demonstrate that ICT integration reshapes reliability boundaries and demands auditable AI–operations interfaces. Prior CPS reliability work has primarily addressed sensing, communication, and protection layers; we extend the same discipline to the decision-support reasoning layer, closing the gap repeatedly identified in the surveys above.
Weaknesses in prior work and motivation
Synthesizing the above, four concrete weaknesses persist: (W1) Fragmented CPS-reliability and reasoning treatment—CPS reliability work10,13,14 models sensing/communication reliability without translating it into reasoning-layer guarantees, while RAG/Self-Refine22,24 optimize text quality without acknowledging upstream cyber conditions. (W2) Weak output governance—existing RAG and CoT systems do not enforce structured field completeness or domain-rule consistency, producing plausible-but-unusable outputs in high-stakes settings. (W3) Loose text–vision coupling—prior power-grid AI21,26,27 treats detection as isolated from textual knowledge. (W4) Domain-agnostic refinement—generic self-refinement24,25 applies uniform critiques regardless of deficiency type. We close (W1)–(W4) by (i) a provenance-tagged knowledge base bridging sensing/communication to reasoning, (ii) explicit five-slot mandatory-field output governance, (iii) shared knowledge between RAT and ACmix detection, and (iv) a domain-aware hierarchical refinement policy that converges in \(\le 3\) iterations on \(98\%\) of cases.

Problem motivation and design rationale before method details
Before detailing each module, we summarize the core design rationale that drives the method: Challenge 1—heterogeneous maintenance records have variable quality and irregular layouts, requiring robust knowledge extraction; Challenge 2—single-pass reasoning often produces incomplete or weakly justified outputs, requiring explicit quality-assured iterative refinement; Challenge 3—small, distant, and occluded visual faults require stronger feature modeling than standard detection pipelines. Therefore, the framework is intentionally partitioned into three coordinated stages: structured knowledge construction, RAT-based quality-assured reasoning, and ACmix-enhanced visual detection.
Acronym clarification used throughout this manuscript: RAG (retrieval-augmented generation), RAT (Recursive Augmented Thinking), CoT (Chain-of-Thought), PMU (phasor measurement unit), DTR (dynamic thermal rating), SIPS (special protection scheme), ICT (information and communication technology), STN (spatial transformer network), SRN (sequence recognition network), NER (named entity recognition), GIS (gas-insulated switchgear), OCR (optical character recognition), LoRA (low-rank adaptation), FAISS (Facebook AI similarity search), mAP (mean average precision), FPS (frames per second), FLOPs (floating-point operations), PPL (perplexity), and TER (translation edit rate).
Stage 1: Structured Knowledge Base Construction - Heterogeneous maintenance documents undergo processing through PP-PicoDet (layout analysis), RARE (text recognition), PMRC (named entity extraction), and MASKER (defect classification). The processing pipeline addresses practical challenges including variable document quality (68% scanned PDFs, 72-600 DPI resolution range), irregular layouts (55% multi-column format), and domain-specific terminology under degraded conditions. Processed information populates a dual-indexed knowledge base: (i) vector database supporting semantic similarity retrieval for contextual case matching; (ii) relational database enabling structured queries for specific equipment types or fault patterns. The resulting knowledge base contains 10,247 processed documents yielding 1,083 structured knowledge entries.
Stage 2: Quality-Assured Strategy Generation - The RAT-enhanced reasoning module implements four sequential steps addressing operational quality requirements: (1) Initial retrieval via semantic similarity matching and keyword filtering from the knowledge base; (2) Chain-of-Thought generation using instruction-tuned Baichuan2-13B with retrieved context, producing structured outputs with intermediate reasoning steps; (3) Three-dimensional quality evaluation assessing mandatory field completeness, content quality confidence, and logical consistency against domain rules; (4) Targeted iterative refinement (up to 3 iterations) addressing identified deficiencies through re-retrieval and regeneration. This design ensures outputs meet completeness and consistency requirements before operator review. The 19.4s average inference time (or 8.3s in fast mode) is suitable for maintenance planning scenarios where decision timescales span minutes to hours.
Stage 3: Visual Detection - ACmix-enhanced YOLOv7 processes inspection imagery, employing hybrid attention mechanisms combining convolutional local feature extraction and self-attention global context modeling to address small-scale and distant defect detection challenges. The visual detection module operates independently but can be used in conjunction with the textual reasoning module for comprehensive fault diagnosis when both text-based case information and visual inspection data are available. All three stages access the centralized knowledge base, ensuring consistent application of domain knowledge across the integrated framework.
Construction of the inspection knowledge base for power grid equipment
The knowledge base framework (Fig. 2) addresses three challenges: multi-format documents with varying quality, irregular text layouts, and domain-specific terminology under degraded conditions. The processing flow (preprocessing \(\rightarrow\) layout parsing \(\rightarrow\) OCR \(\rightarrow\) entity extraction) populates the knowledge base consumed by Stages 2 and 3.
PP-PicoDet34 employs CSP-PAN feature fusion with SimOTA assignment for multi-scale detection, enhanced through: (i) adaptive resolution processing for low-resolution scans, (ii) multi-orientation detection for rotated tables, (iii) hierarchical layout parsing for nested structures. This achieves 94.3% layout accuracy.
RARE35 performs robust text recognition via STN (geometric rectification for distortions, curved text, irregular spacing) and SRN (domain-adaptive features, multi-scale attention, noise-robust encoding), achieving 91.7% character-level accuracy versus 78.3% for generic OCR.
PMRC36 extracts defect-related keywords through adaptive prompt templates handling: multi-template ensemble (formal/colloquial/abbreviated notations), synonym expansion (equipment aliases), and context-aware disambiguation. This achieves 88.6% F1-score across 15+ document types versus 71.4% for standard NER.
MASKER37 categorizes defects via contextual masked reconstruction with: hierarchical defect taxonomy, multi-granularity context modeling, and temporal pattern recognition. It achieves 92.1% classification accuracy, handling noisy inputs including incomplete descriptions and informal annotations.
Data trustworthiness and FDI resilience
Beyond extraction accuracy, the knowledge base attaches three integrity attributes to every structured entry, motivated by FDI mitigation9 and CPS reliability modelling10: (i) a source-channel tag (sensor telemetry, lab-test report, expert annotation, regulatory document); (ii) a cross-source consistency score computed against parallel mentions in adjacent documents in the MASKER similarity space, flagging entries whose normalized inter-source disagreement exceeds 0.3 as low-trust; (iii) a temporal validity window restricting use of regulatory entries to their valid date range. These attributes are exposed as retrievable metadata and consumed by the RAT confidence dimension, so that low-trust entries are deprioritized during evidence aggregation. While runtime FDI detection is out of scope, this design provides the structural hooks for downstream integration with online FDI classifiers (e.g.,9)—realizing the principle, repeatedly emphasized in CPS reliability surveys15,16, that reasoning quality cannot exceed upstream sensing/communication trustworthiness.
Knowledge-driven strategy generation for power grid inspection
This study proposes a lightweight power domain-specific pretraining strategy using Baichuan2-13B38 as backbone. Pretraining on large-scale datasets containing equipment failure descriptions, regulatory documents, and standards imparts domain knowledge while maintaining general-purpose robustness. This minimizes training cost and improves generalization on downstream tasks.
Instruction-based fine-tuning is then performed using domain-specific instructions including decision-making schemes and fault diagnostics39. Structuring training instances as question-answer pairs enables the model to generalize across unseen inspection-related tasks while maintaining a lightweight computation footprint.
To address operational requirements for systematic quality assurance in retrieval-augmented generation for power grid maintenance, we implement a Recursive Augmented Thinking (RAT) mechanism (Figure 3).
Design rationale: Power grid fault diagnosis requires outputs satisfying specific completeness and consistency requirements before operator review: all mandatory decision-support fields must be populated (fault cause, affected component, maintenance actions, risk assessment, reference basis), and recommendations must align with domain operational rules (e.g., correlating dissolved gas patterns with appropriate fault mechanisms). Single-pass generation frequently produces incomplete outputs requiring manual completion or outputs containing logical inconsistencies requiring expert correction. RAT addresses these limitations through systematic evaluation and targeted refinement: (i) generates initial strategies using retrieved knowledge and chain-of-thought reasoning; (ii) evaluates outputs across three dimensions using domain-specific criteria (mandatory field presence, content quality indicators, logical consistency with domain rules); (iii) performs targeted re-retrieval and regeneration addressing identified deficiencies; (iv) iterates (maximum 3 cycles) until quality requirements are met or iteration limit reached.
The RAT mechanism builds upon traditional RAG by adding three components: (1) Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting for structured output generation with intermediate reasoning steps, (2) three-dimensional quality evaluation systematically assessing outputs against operational requirements, and (3) targeted iterative refinement addressing identified deficiencies. The implementation employs external LLMs to generate task-specific prompts for fault diagnosis and maintenance strategy formulation using LangChain and LlamaIndex frameworks. CoT outputs and retrieved historical case information are organized in unified message format for the integrated pipeline, combining retrieved domain knowledge with step-by-step reasoning to provide both contextual information and logical analysis supporting maintenance decisions.

Robustness under communication degradation and partial sensing
Synchrophasor/PMU schemes degrade under partial communication availability13,14, and PMU placement/cybersecurity exposure further shapes downstream observability11,12. We make the RAT loop explicitly degradation-aware via three mechanisms: (i) Trust-weighted retrieval—retrieval similarity in Eqs. (1)/(2)/(4) is multiplied by the Stage 1 provenance trust score, deprioritizing evidence from temporarily unreliable channels and enforcing the surveyed principle15,16 that reasoning confidence must inherit sensing/communication reliability. (ii) Channel-aware confidence penalty—when a recommendation primarily depends on a flagged-unavailable sensor family (e.g., synchrophasor-based DTR during a known outage), \(C_{certain}\) in Eq. (2) is penalized by 0.2 per affected mandatory slot, deliberately driving confidence below 0.65 and triggering RAT to re-retrieve offline-verifiable alternatives (lab analysis, static specifications). (iii) Consistency-rule fallbacks under partial observability—Dimension 3 includes patterns such as “if PMU/synchrophasor evidence is unavailable, disallow conclusions requiring synchrophasor confirmation and prefer offline-verifiable recommendations”, derived from13,14. Together these mechanisms let the system gracefully degrade—rather than silently mis-recommend—under communication degradation, FDI suspicion, or partial sensor availability.

Vision based electric component fault detection
Small electric components and fault points in power grid images pose detection challenges due to their small size and complicated backgrounds. This study introduces the ACmix attention mechanism40 into YOLOv732 to improve small-scale target detection as illustrated in Fig. 5. ACmix balances global and local feature extraction, ensuring sensitivity to fine details for accurate small target localization.
The ACmix module integrates into YOLOv7’s backbone, combining convolutional and self-attention mechanisms. Input feature maps (\(H \times W\times C\)) pass through \(3 \times 3\) convolution and split into N sub-features (\(H\times W\times \frac{C}{N}\)) for multi-scale learning. The convolutional branch captures local contextual information while the self-attention branch obtains global context through feature similarity computation. Outputs are fused with learnable scalars \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\): \(F_{out} = \alpha F_{att} + \beta F_{conv}\).
This hybrid design enhances YOLOv7’s sensitivity to small targets by effectively combining local and global feature representations. The complementary outputs provide spatial detail and contextual semantics, enabling better localization and classification of small-scale objects in complex power grid environments.
Results
We present results in three parts corresponding to the framework stages: knowledge base construction (§3.2), strategy generation with RAT evaluation (§3.3), and visual anomaly detection (§3.4).
Datasets and experimental setup
Knowledge base dataset
10,247 PDF documents from five provincial power grid companies (2018-2023): fault reports (3,842), maintenance logs (4,156), inspection records (1,523), technical specifications (726), processed into 1,083 structured knowledge entries covering 14 equipment categories and 127 fault types. Documents split 80/10/10 (8,198/1,025/1,024) with temporal stratification to prevent data leakage.
Strategy generation dataset
120 real-world fault cases (2022-2023) with expert-validated references, collected independently from the knowledge base documents for evaluation purposes. Each case includes: (i) input fault description with available diagnostic data; (ii) expert-annotated ground truth covering the five mandatory slots (fault cause, affected component, maintenance actions, risk level, reference basis) and free-form diagnostic reports for NLP metric evaluation. These cases cover diverse equipment types and fault complexities (35% single-component, 28% multi-equipment, 18% cascading, 19% planning scenarios).
Comparative baseline configuration
All comparison methods receive identical conditions to ensure fair comparison: (a) Retrieval: same top-5 retrieved documents from the knowledge base via semantic similarity search; (b) Prompting: structured output prompts explicitly requesting the five mandatory slots (fault cause, affected component, maintenance actions, risk level, reference basis) with Chain-of-Thought reasoning instructions; (c) Evaluation: assessed using both domain-specific metrics (slot completeness, confidence, consistency) and standard NLP metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore, BLEURT) against expert-validated references. Single-pass baselines lack systematic multi-dimensional evaluation and iterative refinement. Note that Baichuan2-13B was specifically fine-tuned on the five-slot output structure (8,198 training documents), while API-based baselines (GPT-4, Claude, etc.) received only prompting instructions without domain-specific training. The reported improvements reflect the combined effects of domain fine-tuning, structured training, and the RAT mechanism’s iterative quality assurance, with ablation studies (Table 3 Section C) isolating RAT’s independent contribution.
Anomaly detection dataset
15,648 annotated images from 23 substations with 14 fault classes and 47,231 bounding boxes (38% small objects <32\(^2\) pixels). Data split: 70/15/15 train/val/test.
Experimental configuration
NVIDIA A100 GPUs (40GB). Baichuan2-13B: LoRA fine-tuning (rank=8) for 3 epochs on the 8,198 training documents. RAT: FAISS index with top-k=5, confidence threshold \(\theta _{conf}\)=0.65 (selected via grid search on a development set separate from the 120 test cases). YOLOv7+ACmix: 300 epochs with cosine annealing and multi-scale training on 10,953 training images, with hyperparameters validated on the 2,347-image validation set.
Evaluation metrics
(1) Slot completeness: computed via Equation (1) by checking presence of all five mandatory fields in generated outputs; (2) Confidence scores: self-assessed by the system via Equation (2) during inference, reflecting internal quality estimation (note: these are not calibrated against external ground truth but used for triggering refinement); (3) Logical consistency: verified against 10-pattern rule base derived from domain expert knowledge; (4) Content quality: standard NLP metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore, BLEURT) computed against expert-validated reference texts. For fair comparison, all baselines are evaluated using identical metrics, though only RAT employs self-assessment for iterative refinement.

Clarification on the Ablation rows that look numerically close to full RAT
Reviewer feedback pointed out that several rows in Section C of Table 3 appear numerically similar to Full RAT, which may seem inconsistent with the claim that each evaluation dimension is essential. We explicitly clarify the design reason here, because the visual proximity of numbers can be misleading: the three RAT dimensions are by construction non-redundant, and each ablation only collapses the metric corresponding to the disabled dimension, leaving the other two metrics largely untouched. Specifically, (i) the w/o Slot Completeness Check row degrades primarily on Completeness (\(98\%\rightarrow 65\%\), \(-33\) pts), while Confidence (\(0.82\rightarrow 0.79\)) and Consistency (\(96\%\rightarrow 94\%\)) are nearly unchanged because removing the completeness gate does not break the independent confidence-scoring and consistency-rule pipelines—this is the expected behavior, not an artifact. (ii) The w/o Confidence Analysis row leaves Completeness at 97% and Consistency at 95% because the completeness gate is still actively populating mandatory slots and the rule-based consistency checks still fire; only the confidence dimension is meaningfully removed (shown as “—”). (iii) The w/o Consistency Verification row preserves Completeness (98%) and Confidence (0.81) but collapses Consistency from 96% to 74% (\(-22\) pts), confirming that the consistency dimension is independently responsible for the consistency metric. (iv) Only the w/o Recursive Refinement row degrades all three metrics simultaneously (\(98\%\rightarrow 72\%\), \(0.82\rightarrow 0.61\), \(96\%\rightarrow 78\%\)), which is consistent with the fact that recursive refinement is the global mechanism that enforces all three evaluation dimensions jointly. In other words, the apparent “baseline-like” values in some ablation rows are not contradictions but are diagnostic of dimension-wise orthogonality: each ablation surgically removes one capability, and the metric tied to that capability is the one that drops sharply, while the other two remain close to Full RAT.

                    2.
                    
                      Self-assessment without independent expert calibration. Confidence and consistency scores are produced by the system itself. The 0.4/0.3/0.3 weighting was tuned by grid search on a held-out development set and reviewed by experts; the 10-pattern rule base was manually curated. An inter-rater reliability study against independent expert judgments remains future work.
- 
                    3.
                    
                      Baseline-fairness caveat. Baichuan2-13B was domain-fine-tuned on 8,198 training documents, while API baselines received only prompts. To partly isolate RAT’s contribution, the ablation in Table 3 (Section C) holds domain fine-tuning fixed and removes recursive refinement, yielding \(0.92\rightarrow 0.70\) (\(+31\%\) relative attributable to RAT). Cross-model evaluation (Section D) further shows \(+19\)–\(25\%\) RAT gain across five backbones, evidence of partial generalizability across architectures.
- 
                    4.
                    
                      Computational overhead and model dependency. RAT incurs \(2.4\times\) overhead (19.4 s vs. 8.0 s) and is therefore unsuited to sub-second emergencies; a fast mode at 8.3 s preserves 0.74 confidence (vs. 0.82). The \(+19\)–\(25\%\) spread across backbones indicates that RAT compensates partially, not fully, for weaker base models.
- 
                    5.
                    
                      Knowledge coverage. The 10-pattern rule base covers frequent fault scenarios in the training data; the two non-converging cases out of 120 fall outside this coverage. Automated extraction from larger expert-validated corpora is a concrete next step.
System performance within validated scope
Within power-grid maintenance, the system achieves \(95\%\) output completeness, 0.82 confidence, and \(\approx 98\%\) convergence (118/120 cases) within 3 iterations; visual detection reaches 0.847 small-object mAP and retains \(87.4\%\) of normal-condition performance under occlusion/distance/lighting/weather. Resource usage is moderate (39.1 GB memory, 19.4 s inference), suitable for non-emergency scenarios. Outputs are traceable via per-slot citations to structured knowledge entries.
Generalizability beyond power grids remains unvalidated; cross-domain deployment requires slot-structure redesign, recalibration of evaluation criteria/rules, domain-specific training data, and expert validation studies.
Cyber-physical reliability implications
The framework should be read as an operational reasoning layer that extends established CPS reliability disciplines to the decision-support layer. (i) Data trustworthiness / FDI resilience: Stage 1’s provenance-aware knowledge base (source-channel tag, cross-source consistency score, temporal validity window) is structurally aligned with9,10; once a sensor stream is flagged compromised, all derived entries are deprioritized in retrieval, preventing the reasoning module from amplifying corrupted upstream data. (ii) Communication-availability awareness: motivated by13,14, the channel-aware confidence penalty and consistency-rule fallbacks (Method) cause the system to re-retrieve offline-verifiable evidence rather than emit a plausible-but-unfounded recommendation when a relied-upon channel is degraded—to our knowledge the first reasoning-layer mechanism propagating communication availability into LLM output gating in this context. (iii) PMU/synchrophasor cybersecurity:11,12 motivate separating PMU- and non-PMU-sourced evidence into trust groups, so that operators can audit afterwards whether a recommendation inherited any PMU-related cybersecurity exposure. (iv) Auditable ICT-integrated operation:15,16 call for auditable AI–operations interfaces; the five-slot mandatory output (cause, component, action, risk, reference) supplies exactly such an audit chain by pairing every recommendation with a citation to a specific structured entry, traceable through the provenance tag back to the originating channel.
Future research directions
Key directions include: (1) Human validation studies comparing system assessments against independent expert judgments to calibrate self-assessment metrics and establish inter-rater reliability, addressing current reliance on internal evaluation criteria; (2) Computational optimization through lightweight evaluation methods and adaptive mechanisms adjusting refinement stringency based on risk factors, reducing the 2.4\(\times\) overhead for time-sensitive scenarios; (3) Automated knowledge engineering extracting consistency patterns from larger expert-validated corpora to expand coverage beyond the current 10-pattern rule base, addressing rare and novel fault types; (4) Controlled ablation experiments comparing domain-trained baselines with and without RAT to more precisely quantify RAT’s isolated contribution; (5) Long-term deployment studies tracking operator acceptance, intervention rates, and decision quality in operational environments to validate practical utility beyond controlled test conditions.
Practical recommendations
Based on the validated experimental scope, we recommend: (1) deploy RAT full mode for planned maintenance and post-event diagnosis where quality assurance is prioritized; (2) use fast mode for time-critical triage, followed by deferred full-mode verification for final reporting; (3) establish periodic expert review cycles to recalibrate confidence thresholds and update consistency rule patterns; (4) expand knowledge base coverage for rare fault types through structured expert curation; (5) integrate communication-health monitoring to flag reduced trust in upstream sensing/telemetry during strategy generation.
Conclusion
This paper proposes a knowledge-guided multimodal reasoning framework for intelligent power-grid maintenance that integrates a provenance-aware structured knowledge base, the Recursive Augmented Thinking (RAT) reasoning module with three-dimensional quality evaluation, and an ACmix-enhanced YOLOv7 visual detector under a unified cyber-physical reliability perspective. The three-dimensional evaluation (mandatory five-slot completeness, weighted confidence with 0.4/0.3/0.3 aggregation, rule-based logical consistency) and the hierarchical refinement policy distinguish our work from generic single-pass RAG and free-form self-refinement methods.
Quantitative improvements (numerical, vs. baselines)
On 120 expert-validated fault cases, the proposed system achieves the following measurable gains: (i) output completeness \(95\%\) vs. \(65\%\) for vanilla RAG (\(+30\) pts, \(+46\%\) relative) and vs. \(71\%\) for RAG+CoT (\(+24\) pts, \(+34\%\) relative); (ii) self-evaluated confidence 0.82 vs. 0.55 for vanilla RAG (\(+0.27\), \(+49\%\) relative) and vs. 0.65 for Self-Refine (\(+0.17\), \(+26\%\) relative); (iii) logical consistency \(93\%\)+ vs. \(70\%\)–\(82\%\) for the four RAG variants (\(+11\) to \(+23\) pts); (iv) ROUGE-1 F1 0.859, BERTScore F1 0.981, and BLEURT 0.610 vs. the best API baseline (Chat4o-mini: ROUGE-1 F1 0.704, BERTScore F1 0.938, BLEURT 0.554), yielding relative improvements of \(+22.0\%\), \(+4.6\%\), and \(+10.1\%\) respectively; (v) approximately \(98\%\) convergence rate (118/120 cases) within 3 iterations, with \(78.3\%\) of cases converging by iteration 2. On the 2, 347-image visual test set, the ACmix-enhanced YOLOv7 reaches mAP@.5 0.952 vs. 0.921 baseline (\(+3.1\) pts), small-object mAP 0.847 vs. 0.731 (\(+11.6\) pts), and retains \(87.4\%\) of normal-condition performance under occlusion/distance/lighting/weather, outperforming YOLOv8 by \(+4.4\) pts and DINO-5scale by \(+2.0\) pts on the averaged challenging-condition mAP.
Quantitative limitations
The reported gains are accompanied by three measurable costs: (i) RAT incurs a \(2.4\times\) computation overhead (19.4 s vs. 8.0 s vanilla RAG), partially mitigated by a fast mode of 8.3 s with a graceful confidence drop of \(0.82\rightarrow 0.74\); (ii) the cross-LLM gain of RAT varies between \(+19\%\) and \(+25\%\) across five backbones, indicating residual dependence on base-model capability; (iii) 2/120 cases (\(1.7\%\)) failed to converge within the iteration budget, concentrated in rare fault types outside the current 10-pattern rule base.
Concrete future directions
Three quantitatively scoped directions remain: (a) reducing the \(2.4\times\) overhead toward \(\le 1.5\times\) via lightweight evaluators and adaptive iteration budgeting; (b) expanding the consistency rule base from 10 to a target of \(\ge 50\) patterns through automated extraction from larger expert-validated corpora, aiming to push the convergence rate from \(98.3\%\) to \(\ge 99.5\%\); (c) conducting an inter-rater reliability study with \(\ge 10\) domain experts to calibrate the 0.65 confidence threshold against independent human judgment. Together, these results position the proposed framework as a quantitatively validated reasoning layer that extends established cyber-physical reliability disciplines into AI-driven maintenance decision support.
Data Availability
The datasets generated and/or analysed during the current study are not publicly available due to confidentiality agreements and critical infrastructure protection regulations associated with proprietary operational systems of power grid companies, but are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.

title: The future of energy is now
content:
The future of energy is now
June 12, 2026Newsletter Archives
Some weeks slip by unnoticed, while others make a real impact. With GM Empower kicking off on Tuesday, this week was an example of the latter. Empower laid a roadmap toward a bright future, when EVs and their batteries work together to bolster our power grid. Together, the pair are powerful enough to help address the unprecedented energy challenges of our time.
Itâs all thanks to GMâs Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) technology. Want to know how this so-called âbidirectionalâ charging system actually works? Weâre glad you asked.
At its core, V2G can connect your compatible GM EV to the local power grid (where available) with a proper grid interconnection. This allows your vehicle to help power your properly equipped home during outages, but can also to send energy back to the grid through participating utilities when demand is high.1 This bidirectional energy flow can help lend stability to a national grid in desperate need of modernization.
To be clear, V2G tech has the potential to revolutionize our lives.
In a call-to-action, GM Energy vice president Wade Sheffer outlined the benefits for energy customers, legislators, and utilities providers alike. With more than 250,000 bidirectional-capable GM EVs currently on the road, V2Gâs potential is already parked in our driveways, just waiting to be unleashed.
When paired with grid storage solutions like GM next-generation sodium-ion battery cells V2G technology can help pave the way to a more advanced, efficient, resilient grid for all.
But that wasnât all from Empower. Some of the biggest news from the event fits right in your pocket. Meet Energy Pass, an easier way to charge your EV on the go. In practical terms, Energy Pass means less spent time managing charging logistics, more charging flexibility, and less time sitting still.
Now that's some news that won't slip by unnoticed.
Be empowered,
âKyle Kinard, Managing Editor, GM News
